<Conflicting opinions and research outcomes> — Some studies claim hot drinks can cool you down under specific conditions, while other research finds no extra cooling effect compared to cold drinks.

The retrieved documents present conflicting scientific findings. d1, d3, d4, d5, d6, d8, d10, and d11 cite studies (often from the University of Ottawa) concluding that hot drinks can cool the body by increasing sweat evaporation, provided conditions are dry. In contrast, d7 reports an experiment showing a hot drink did not cool the participant more than a cold drink, and cites a larger Australian study finding the body maintains core temperature regardless of drink temperature. d9 (NHS) advises avoiding hot drinks to cope with heat. These are contradictory research outcomes within the same scope.

The evidence is divided, so a definitive yes/no answer is not possible from the retrieved set. The conflict type requires presenting the differing perspectives neutrally. The answer will summarize the two main opposing research conclusions found in the documents.

Hot drinks may cool you down under specific dry conditions, according to several studies [d1, d3, d5, d6]. These studies found that a hot drink triggers increased sweating, and if that sweat can evaporate, it removes more heat than the drink adds [d1, d4, d11]. However, other research contradicts this: a BBC experiment found a hot drink did not provide more cooling than a cold drink [d7], and an Australian study concluded the body maintains its core temperature regardless of drink temperature [d7]. Official health advice also recommends avoiding hot drinks during heatwaves [d9]. Therefore, scientific opinion is divided on whether hot drinks are an effective cooling method.
